Crop the images

Source: R/crop-zoom.R
add_crop.Rd

add_crop() shows a region of each image instead of the full image. The size of the region is the same for all images, so all panels share the same magnification; only its position can differ between images.

Usage

add_crop(
  montage,
  width,
  height = width,
  center = c(0.5, 0.5),
  units = c("um", "px"),
  center_units = c("rel", "px"),
  name = "crop",
  angle = NULL
)

Arguments

montage

A tidymontage() object.

width, height

Size of the region. In micrometres by default, which keeps the magnification equal even if images have different pixel sizes.

center

Position of the region's center: a numeric vector c(x, y) used for all images, or a data frame with columns x, y and one or more columns of the images tibble to match on, e.g. condition or filepath. The data frame can also have an angle column, for a different angle per image.

units

Units of width and height: "um" (micrometres, needs a known pixel size) or "px" (pixels).

center_units

Units of center: "rel" (relative, 0-1) or "px".

name

Name of the view in the layout.

angle

Rotation of the region in degrees, counterclockwise, as Fiji measures the angle of a line. NULL (the default) means no rotation, unless center has an angle column.

Value

The montage with the crop step added.

Details

Positions are given as the center of the region, either one position for all images or a data frame with one position per image or group. By default, positions are relative to the full image (0 = left or top edge, 1 = right or bottom edge); with center_units = "px" they are pixel coordinates of the full image, counted from 0 as in ImageJ / Fiji.

Display ranges are always computed from the full images, so moving a crop doesn't change brightness.

A montage has one crop: calling add_crop() again replaces the earlier crop. Use add_zoom() for further regions.

With angle, the region is rotated, for structures that run at an angle, such as a neurite. The angle is the one Fiji reports for a line drawn along the structure (Analyze > Measure): in degrees, counterclockwise. The region's width runs along that line, and the panel shows it upright, so the structure lies horizontal. Rotated regions are sampled with bilinear interpolation, at the original pixel size. Unlike upright regions, they are not moved inside the image: all their corners must lie within it.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
centers <- tibble::tibble(condition = c("ctrl", "ko"), x = c(0.4, 0.6), y = c(0.5, 0.3))
montage |> add_crop(width = 40, center = centers)

# rotated, with an angle per image
centers$angle <- c(30, -15)
montage |> add_crop(width = 40, center = centers)
} # }
